newsitem.title: USA: Staples - fight for the mind of FTC Chairman.
newsitem.headline: Staples - fight for the mind of FTC Chairman.

text.p: Antitrust experts believe the Federal Trade Commission may still approve a restructured Staples Inc. office superstore merger, despite a statement suggesting otherwise by FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky.
Pitofsky was questioned hours after the FTC voted Monday, 4-1, to seek a court order blocking the $4 billion merger of Staples and Office Depot Inc..

"Prices are higher in those cities where there is one superstore, office supply superstore, than where there are two. And they're higher in cities where their are two superstore office supply firms than where there are three," he told CNBC.

The name of the game in antitrust is to achieve lower prices for consumers. A merger between Staples and Office Depot would diminish the number of office superstores chains to two. The other is OfficeMax Inc..

"If (Pitofsky) adheres to that statement he has to reject the deal," said James Love, an economist with Ralph Nader's Center for Study of Responsive Law. "And we don't know what he's going to do. But I think that he was right on Monday."

Pitofsky, a giant in the field of antitrust, has in the past generally been able to swing a majority of the commission his way. Although no one knows, there are suggestions that Pitofsky may approve the deal despite his statement.
For one thing, people close to the talks say the FTC was ready to approve the merger if Staples and Office Depot divested 62 stores to OfficeMax, but the chains could not make a deal.

After the commission voted, the three stores reached agreement Wednesday for Staples and Office Depot to divest 63 stores -- in nearly the same mix as the 62 earlier stores -- to OfficeMax for $108.75 million.
So will the FTC now approve the merger?

By its own lights, if the FTC approves the new agreement, it is "tacitly acknowledging it is going to allow the merger to lead to some price increases," said Kevin Arquit, a former senior FTC official now in private practice with the Rogers & Wells firm in New York.
"What that means is that they assessed the litigation risk and decided the perfect should not be the enemy of the good," Arquit said.
The FTC reportedly has documents that some inside the agency believe will convince a judge of its positions, while others are not as sure.
"It sounds to me like they're close to cutting a deal," said Steve Axxin of the firm Skadden & Arps in New York.
But Axxin said whether or not the merger wins approval the fact that it has gone this far has important implications for the antitrust field.
In the past, the FTC generally went to court when it believed a retailer held a huge percentage of the market.

Staples and Office Depot have argued that they have only a very small percentage of the market for office supplies, computers and other office products. But it may now be true that the market definition is beside the point, Axxin said.

"If you have direct evidence that prices will go up or consumer choice will go down, then you can skip the whole market definition step," he said. "Thirty years ago, people were writing law review articles about that. Now, the chickens are coming home to roost."
